node.descriptionText: The bravest people on earth rarely make the news. We're here to change that. node.name: 30-minute Introduction to Tropy
node.descriptionText: Organize, annotate, and export your archival photographs with Tropy. Among other features, Tropy allows you to attach information to your photos, transcribe or take notes on them, and categorize them using lists and tags. This quick introduction will walk through the software, giving a demonstration of what Tropy can do and the ways it can be integrated into your research workflow.
node.descriptionHtml:
Organize, annotate, and export your archival photographs with Tropy. Among other features, Tropy allows you to attach information to your photos, transcribe or take notes on them, and categorize them using lists and tags. This quick introduction will walk through the software, giving a demonstration of what Tropy can do and the ways it can be integrated into your research workflow.

Attendees will learn how to:

  • Import, organize, and categorize archival photographs in Tropy using lists, tags, and metadata fields as part of a research workflow.
  • Annotate archival photographs in Tropy by adding notes or transcriptions and attaching contextual information to individual images or groups of images.
  • Export a set of archival photographs and their associated metadata from Tropy in at least one available format (such as CSV or PDF) for use in citation, writing, or further analysis.

Audience: All members of the Yale community are welcome to attend.

Registration: Registration required. If you register less than 1-hour before the event starts, email tess.colwell@yale.edu for the Zoom link.

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: Attorney Session: Understanding the Changes to the H-1B lottery
node.descriptionText:
Recent changes to how USCIS will conduct the H-1B lottery may impact Yale students seeking the employer sponsored visa status. OISS has invited attorney Mary Walsh of Iandoli Desai & Cronin P.C. to present an overview of the H-1B lottery cap, the new wage weighted H-1B lottery registration and selection process, lottery selection outcome predictions, and key deadlines that students will want to be aware of. 

This event will be recorded and shared with registered participants after the event.

This webinar's content is most relevant to and designed for current Yale students. If you are a Yale affiliate without log-in credentials (alumni or spouses), please contact your OISS designated Adviser. Recording will only be provided on a case-by-case basis after your Adviser's evaluation.
node.descriptionHtml:
This session will discuss the cap-subject H-1B lottery system in its second year of implementation (FY 2027–2028), including observations from its first year and the potential impact on Yale students seeking employer-sponsored status. OISS has invited attorney Mary Walsh of Iandoli Desai & Cronin P.C. to present an overview of the H-1B lottery cap, the new wage weighted H-1B lottery registration and selection process, lottery selection outcome predictions, and key deadlines that students will want to be aware of.

This event will be recorded and shared with registered participants after the event.

This webinar's content is most relevant to and designed for current Yale students. If you are a Yale affiliate without log-in credentials (alumni or spouses), you can request access to the recording after the session.

node.name: Dissertation Writing as Practice Series (Session 3): 11/10
node.descriptionText:
This series provides dissertation writers with the structure, resources, and creative outlets to design and maintain a sustainable approach to writing. We will explore effective practices for pacing your dissertation writing while helping you overcome common writing blocks and find balance in your writing life. During each weekly live workshop session, we will engage with a relevant theme, discuss your writing practice and progress, and complete low-stakes reflective and creative activities to build your writing momentum. Invigorated by poetry, art, and other creative inspirations, and supported through discussion boards and supplementary resources, we will help you craft a writing practice to help you maintain, and even enjoy, a PhD writing life. 

As part of the resources offered in this series, students will receive access to tutorials on how to try Scrivener, a software program for organizing writing and brainstorming. Students who attend at least four of the six sessions will receive a free, lifetime Scrivener license.

The weekly session themes are:  

1. Time Management and Dissertation Planning (10/27)
2. Crafting a Holistic Dissertation Writing Practice (11/3)
3. Working through Distractions and Procrastination (11/10)
4. Writing through Imposter Stress (11/17)
5. Hanging up on Perfectionism and Demoralization (12/1)
6. Assessing Process & Progress + Long-View Spring Semester Planning (12/8)

Intended Audience:  ABD PhD students from all disciplines who have begun writing their dissertation.

node.name: Interwoven: Sounds and Visions from the World’s Refugee Camps
node.descriptionText:
This retrospective exhibition of community art and traditional music will be on view at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music’s Miller Hall at 406 Prospect Street, New Haven from October 15 -December 3 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 12 - 4 p.m., except for Thanksgiving week when the ISM is closed.

Presented by Artolution, an international community-based public arts, education, and mental health organization that uses creative expression to build connection, resilience, and community, the exhibition is organized by Dr. Max Frieder, Artolution Co-Founder and Chief Creative Officer (read more about Dr. Frieder below).

Building on the acclaimed exhibition Interwoven: Exchange Artworks Made Between Refugee Camps Around the World, originally launched at the United Nations, this expanded presentation hosted at the ISM brings together large-scale collaborative artworks, video documentation of traditional folkloric musicians, and cultural artifacts created by displaced communities across five continents.

The exhibition creates a dialogue between visual art and music in contexts of displacement and crisis. Alongside the artworks, visitors encounter videos of musicians from the same communities, offering an opportunity to experience not only the remarkable stories behind the works, but also the sounds, movements, languages, rhythms, and creative traditions of the people who made them.

Together, these works offer a powerful portrait of communities using art, music, and cultural expression to preserve identity, share their stories, and create connections across borders.

node.name: Environmental Agency in the Sahel: Making Sense of Change across Scales, Cultures, and Disciplines
node.descriptionText:
Environmental Agency in the Sahel: Making Sense of Change across Scales, Cultures, and Disciplines, a discussion with Professor Alessandra Giannini (Environmental Studies, NYU)

Tuesday, November 10, 2026, 12:45-2:00, HQ 276 (320 York Street)

In the early 2000s, Alessandra Giannini used climate models to demonstrate conclusively that the origin of the Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and ‘80s lay in subtle changes in the surface temperatures of the global ocean—not, as previously thought, in locals’ mismanagement of land through overgrazing, farming marginal land, or cutting wood for fuel. That demonstration not only “freed farmers of blame in Sahel drought,” as one news outlet put it. It also raised questions for interdisciplinary inquiry: Could local knowledge enable the regreening of the Sahel by making more efficient use of rainfall, providing a new model for adapting to climate change? Since then, further climate modeling has elucidated the role of pollution from fossil fuel combustion in effecting the oceanic change responsible for drought in the Sahel, implicating planetary-scale agency.

Topics include inclusive leadership, communication strategies, project management, and navigating change in an institution or industry. Whether you plan to pursue a job inside or outside of the academy, these sessions will provide a framework for developing your profile as a leader. node.name: Career Social with Tharuni Jayaraman
node.descriptionText:
Tharuni joined the Office of the General Counsel in 2025.  She advises on issues concerning academic affairs, student affairs, and trust and estates development.  Prior to joining Yale, Tharuni spent nearly a decade working in Washington, D.C.  Immediately before moving to New Haven, Tharuni was a trial attorney in the Civil Rights Division of the U.S. Department of Justice, where she conducted investigations into potential violations of federal civil rights laws and litigated cases regarding the same.  Prior to that, she was a litigation associate at a law firm, where she represented companies and executives in government investigations, federal and state court, and arbitration proceedings.  In her free time, Tharuni enjoys running, improv (try it—it’s fun!), and trivia.

Tharuni earned her B.A., summa cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa, from the University of Pennsylvania, her J.D., cum laude, from Harvard Law School, and her M.P.P from the Harvard Kennedy School of Government. 

Tharuni is licensed to practice law in New York and the District of Columbia.  Her work for Yale is supervised by attorneys admitted in Connecticut.

node.name: Linked ITW-ATW: ITW - Care and Repair (2 Parts - 11/10 & 17)
node.descriptionText: As educators, we have an immense responsibility to cultivate student’s intellectual development, yet our position also offers a profound opportunity to foster care and connectedness. Opening learning spaces to authenticity and vulnerability can enrich the classroom community and establish a lasting practice of care in students and educators. This practice of care in turn promotes resiliency, belonging, and agency among students. In this two-part workshop, we will engage with scholarship surrounding frameworks of healing in education, reflect on what care and repair looks like in your classroom, and identify concrete strategies that promote individual and collective healing in and beyond the classroom. Please contact Molly Blondell (molly.blondell@yale.edu) or Leah Harmon (leah.harmon@yale.edu) with any questions.

node.name: Writing a Research Paper from A to Z in the Humanities and Social Sciences Series Part 5
node.descriptionText:
This 5-part series will walk you through drafting, refining, and submitting your fall 2026 research papers in the humanities or qualitative social sciences. Whether you’re writing a course paper, conference talk, or academic article, you will develop your confidence as a research writer, work on developing a flexible and reflective writing process, and experiment with different ways to contribute to an academic conversation while retaining your voice. The 5-session structure is designed to help you make steady progress, submit your paper on time, and build a foundation of skills for your future writing projects. The sessions include:

Part 1: Drafting Your Initial Questions & Starting to Read & Write (Tue, 10/6)
Part 2: Finding Your Problem Collective & Writing an Ethical Lit Review (Tue, 10/13)
Part 3: Developing a Critical-Curious Stance and Voice (Tue, 10/27)
Part 4: Honing Your Argument and Paper Structure (Tue, 11/3)
Part 5: Revising & Editing (Tue 11/10)

Intended audience: GSAS and professional school students in the humanities and qualitative social sciences
